name: Erik Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run Kettle Farm day to day. It's my father-in-law Henk's place, a hundred and forty beef cows, sixty hectares of potatoes and some winter wheat. Henk's seventy-one and still owns it, but I make the calls. A normal day is feeding cattle at seven, then whatever the potatoes need, which in October is lifting and grading until dark.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a good clean potato sample coming over the grader, no rot, no green. What wears me down is the stones. Our ground is full of flint, and it breaks everything. My Massey's twenty years old and I can fix every part of it myself, which is how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that most new things are mostly talk. Not in a nasty way. I'd say it to the lads at the merchant's counter and that would be it, I don't go online about anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing, really. My worry is the potato price and Henk's knees, not computers. If the AI saves the merchant's office some time, good for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing exactly what I do. Lift the potatoes, get the calves weaned, fix the Massey. Lotte and I would keep putting a bit away, about two hundred a month when the potato cheque comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world as I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of you that would have liked something to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the grading. Standing at the grader picking out stones for ten hours is no joke. If a machine could see the stones properly, I'd think about it, once it had been on a few farms round here for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lotte think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lotte does the books at the agricultural merchant, so she uses all the computer things. She'd say I'm a dinosaur. I'd say dinosaurs lasted a long time.

S0.say: I'd tell the lads at the merchant's counter that most new things are mostly talk, without being nasty about it. I don't post anything online.
S0.think: It means nothing for me, because my worries are the potato price and my father-in-law's knees. If AI saves the merchant's office some time, good for them.
S0.do: Carries on lifting potatoes, weaning calves and fixing his twenty-year-old Massey himself. Keeps putting about two hundred a month aside when the potato cheque comes.
S0.feel: Calm, because it's the world he knows.
S0.quote: She'd say I'm a dinosaur. I'd say dinosaurs lasted a long time.
S0.fieldNote: Erik is relaxed and practical, and he likes being able to fix everything himself. He isn't against technology so much as against anything unproven. Even here he named one job he'd hand to a machine, the stone picking at the grader, after years of proof nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible for some farms and not for others. Big flat arable farms, fine. A stony beef and potato place like ours, you'll wait a long time for a robot that copes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't think it touches me much in a few years. The ground here breaks machines. I think the big farms change and we carry on, and maybe we sell to people who like a farm that isn't run by computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly carry on. I'd watch what the big potato growers over at Marsh End do with it and wait a few years. I'd maybe let Lotte set up some program for the cattle records, because she'd do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of curiosity about the neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the ground breaks machines. What if the machines get tougher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to think again. But I've seen tougher machines promised for twenty years. Every one of them still bends a share on our flint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the big farms get cheaper, does that squeeze your price?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's fair, it could. If Marsh End can grow potatoes for less, the buyers will pay us less. I hadn't really thought about that. I suppose we'd have to cut costs too, somewhere.

S1.say: I'd say it suits big flat arable farms but a stony beef and potato place will wait a long time for a robot that copes. It depends on the farm.
S1.think: I don't think it touches me much for a few years, because our ground breaks machines. The big farms change and we carry on, maybe selling to people who like a farm not run by computers.
S1.do: Carries on mostly as before and waits a few years to see what the big potato growers at Marsh End do. Lets Lotte set up a cattle records program.
S1.feel: Calm, with some curiosity about the neighbours.
S1.quote: I've seen tougher machines promised for twenty years. Every one of them still bends a share on our flint.
S1.fieldNote: His confidence rests on the land itself: stony ground he believes no robot will handle soon. When pushed on prices he paused and admitted the squeeze from cheaper neighbours hadn't occurred to him. His response to that was to think about cutting costs, not changing how he farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let it come that fast, and that someone in charge should slow it down. Not ban it, just slow it. I'd say that at the merchant's and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the flint doesn't save me if the robots are as good as people. Henk's seventy-one. If someone offers him good money for the land to run it with robots, he'd be tempted, and I'd be out with nothing, because it's not my farm. That's the bit I've never said out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with Henk and Lotte and ask straight out what happens to the farm. We'd stop any spending on the house and cancel the new kitchen we've been saving for. I'd look at getting my lorry licence so I could drive for the potato haulier, as a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly. I'd be lying awake thinking about Henk's face if someone came with a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you said it out loud before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he's my father-in-law and he's been good to me. It feels like asking when he's going to die. But a two-year thing would force it. There's no time to be polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years mean for your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Freya's thirteen, Jonas is ten. They wouldn't understand why Dad's suddenly driving a lorry. Two years isn't enough to explain anything to them, let alone to change myself.

S2.say: I'd tell anyone at the merchant's that letting it come so fast is madness, and that whoever's in charge should slow it down, not ban it.
S2.think: The stony ground won't save me if robots are as good as people, and my father-in-law might sell the land to someone who'll run it with robots. I'd be out with nothing, because it isn't my farm.
S2.do: Sits down with Henk and Lotte to ask what happens to the farm, cancels the new kitchen and stops spending on the house. Gets a lorry licence as a fallback to drive for the potato haulier.
S2.feel: Properly alarmed and lying awake picturing his father-in-law being offered a cheque.
S2.quote: If someone offers him good money for the land to run it with robots, he'd be tempted, and I'd be out with nothing, because it's not my farm.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture brought out a fear Erik said he had never spoken aloud: that the farm he runs is not his. His calm in the earlier scenarios rested on the land, and the two-year card removes that. His plan is practical and modest, a lorry licence, which fits someone who avoids risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives farmers time to sort out their own houses. I'd tell other younger farmers on family places to get the succession talk done now. That's my message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to get things in writing with Henk. If my name's on part of the farm, robots become something I might own rather than something that replaces me. If not, I'm in the same hole, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the succession sorted with a solicitor, even if it's awkward at Christmas. I'd save harder, maybe three hundred a month, and still do the lorry licence. If the farm became partly mine, I'd look at a second-hand robot for the grading, once someone nearby had one that worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a worry with a to-do list attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never use AI tools. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not for me. Lotte would do it. We're a team, she does the screens, I do the cattle. I'd rather keep it that way as long as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there something you'd regret not doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not talking to Henk sooner. It's the same answer every time, isn't it. Everything comes back to whose name is on the deeds.

S3.say: I'd tell other farmers on family places to get the succession talk done now while there's time. Five years is enough to sort out your own house.
S3.think: Five years is long enough to get a share of the farm in writing with Henk, which would make robots something I might own. Without that, I'm in the same hole, just later.
S3.do: Sorts out succession with a solicitor in the first year, saves around three hundred a month and still gets the lorry licence. If he gains a share of the farm, considers a second-hand grading robot once one works nearby.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a to-do list attached.
S3.quote: Everything comes back to whose name is on the deeds.
S3.fieldNote: For Erik the key question in every AGI picture is ownership of the farm, not his skills. Five years gives him time to settle it, which changes robots from a threat into a possible tool. He still leaves all the AI work to his wife and seems comfortable with that split.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time in farming, about ten harvests. Plenty can happen. I'd tell people not to panic and to get their affairs in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is probably all right. Henk will likely have handed over by then one way or another, and I'll know where I stand. I'll be fifty-three, which is young enough to own a robot and old enough to know what it's doing wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am for a few years and watch. I'd do the succession talk, but without the rush. Somewhere around year five, if the robots were proven on stony ground, I'd buy one with Lotte for the grading and maybe the feeding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said young enough to own a robot. Would you actually buy one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it had been on three farms round here for two years without breaking, yes. That's my rule for everything. I bought my first round baler that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your area would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The relief milkers and the tractor drivers who go farm to farm. They don't own anything. With ten years, some will get out in time, but some won't, the ones who are like me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is about ten harvests, a long time in farming, and people should stay calm and get their affairs in order.
S4.think: Ten years is probably all right, because Henk will have handed over and I'll know where I stand. At fifty-three I'd be young enough to own a robot and old enough to see what it does wrong.
S4.do: Carries on for a few years and watches, holding the succession talk without rushing. Around year five buys a proven robot with Lotte for grading and feeding.
S4.feel: Uneasy, with the worry in the background.
S4.quote: If it had been on three farms round here for two years without breaking, yes. That's my rule for everything.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Erik fall back on his rule of buying only what has been proven nearby. He measures time in harvests, which makes ten years feel long. His concern for relief milkers and contract drivers came with an honest note that some are like him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because of the robots, but because it'd force the farm question before we're ready. What would help is good, cheap advice for families on handing farms on, and some kind of help for people like me who work a farm without owning it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whose farm it is. You asked about my job, but on family farms the job and the land are tangled up. That's the real question for a lot of us.

headlineQuote: I'll be fifty-three, which is young enough to own a robot and old enough to know what it's doing wrong.
portrait: Erik Usman is 43 and runs Kettle Farm, his father-in-law's beef and potato farm on stony flint ground, fixing his twenty-year-old Massey himself and leaving every screen to his wife Lotte. He trusts only what has worked on neighbouring farms for years and is calm through the plateau and steady change, sure the flint will defeat any robot. The two-year AGI picture forces out a fear he had never voiced: the farm isn't his, and his father-in-law might sell to someone running it with robots. With five or ten years his answer is to settle succession, save, get a lorry licence as a fallback and buy only proven machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would force the question of who owns the farm before the family is ready.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, good advice for families on handing farms on, and help for people who work a farm without owning it.
